title: Who Is Watching the Agents
description: Ten tools built for the part of agent work nobody demos: knowing which agent is stuck, which one spent your budget, and what it actually ran.
content:
# Who Is Watching the Agents

Every agent demo ends the same way: the thing works, the terminal scrolls, someone claps. Nobody shows the twenty minutes afterwards, when four sessions sit half-finished on four machines and you cannot remember which one was waiting on a permission prompt.

That gap is now its own product category. The ten tools below all assume the agent runs fine and ask a different question — can you see it, name it, stop it, and explain what it did? None of them generate code. All of them exist because generation is no longer the hard part.

## The fleet view

[[link:/tools/2229|Flightdeck]] is the most complete answer here. It is a self-hosted observability and control plane: every LLM call, MCP event and tool call streams to a per-agent timeline and a live fleet-wide feed. The part that matters is that budgets act rather than report — warn at 80 percent, swap to a cheaper model at 90, block at 100, all enforced in-process. You can also allowlist or blocklist MCP servers per flavor, so a misconfigured server is stopped before the call leaves the process. It is Apache 2.0 and the sensor wraps your existing SDK clients with an init and a patch.

[[link:/tools/2222|Beeuni]] takes the same problem from the environment side. Instead of observing agents on your laptop, it gives them a computer: an isolated execution environment with persistent files, agent identities, skills, memory and scoped tool permissions defined in a beeuni.yaml. Credentials stay brokered and are never copied into a session, and agents can propose changes to their own instructions that you review before they stick.

## The one that is waiting on you

The most common failure in agent work is not a bad output. It is an agent sitting idle behind a prompt you never saw.

[[link:/tools/2221|Evlat]] solves exactly that with a thin strip on the edge of a Mac screen showing every agent state — waiting, working, done, idle — and one click back to the right iTerm, Warp, Ghostty, VS Code or tmux pane. It also covers anything long-running through evlat watch, including jobs on servers reached over ssh, and it dims a row and says so when a remote link drops rather than showing stale state.

[[link:/tools/2230|barn]] does the menu-bar version: one dot per agent, coral when it needs you, a Spotlight-style switcher on a keyboard shortcut, and a floating deck of status tiles that stays on top across desktops. It reads the process table and agents' own session files, so there is no setup, and nothing leaves the machine.

[[link:/tools/2218|CodeConnect]] pushes the same idea to a phone. Every coding agent on your Mac or Linux machines appears on one screen, and the one waiting on you comes first. The exact command is shown in full, never shortened, with its risk level — a read is one tap, a git push --force needs a deliberate hold and Face ID. It runs over your own tailnet rather than a relay.

## Naming the work

[[link:/tools/2220|rostr]] is a small CLI plus hooks that gives each session a name from a roster you pick, so a notification from Samwise tells you which session sent it. Sessions draft a name when they start and return it to the bench when they end. It sounds like a novelty and behaves like memory: humans remember names, not abstract workstreams.

[[link:/tools/2219|Umtri]] applies the same principle to the codebase. You connect a token to your agent, say "draw my project on Umtri", and get a tree from app down to function, with lines showing how far a change reaches and bugs pinned where they happen. The record survives a forgotten conversation, which is the thing chat history never does.

## Catching what the agent broke

[[link:/tools/2215|Chemical X]] is an architecture layer that fights context burn. A SQLite symbol index answers queries so the agent reads symbols instead of whole files, and its site reports roughly 12 tokens for a verification turn that costs about 12,960 through a raw test run. AST rules gate task completion, so an agent cannot mark work done while violating structure.

[[link:/tools/2233|GenClass]] looks at the class of bug tests structurally miss. One import records user actions, async work, network traffic, store writes and errors, then a small model running in a Web Worker over WebGPU or WASM decides what is happening and which action is best. In guard mode it can stop a stale response or double submit before the user sees it. It is Apache 2.0, and anonymous diagnostics are on by default — worth turning off deliberately.

[[link:/tools/2247|ForensicDbg]] handles the other end: native Windows x64 and x86 crashes analysed after the fact, with visual debugging, an AI debugging mode and an MCP setup guide for agents. It is in private beta, so treat it as a look at where post-mortem tooling is heading.

## What this group says

Read together, these tools describe a shift in what counts as agent infrastructure. Two years ago the interesting question was whether a model could write the function. Now the interesting question is whether you can find the session, name it, cap its spend, and read back the exact call that broke staging at 2am.

[[link:/tools/2229|Flightdeck]] and [[link:/tools/2221|Evlat]] answer the first two. [[link:/tools/2220|rostr]] and [[link:/tools/2219|Umtri]] make the fleet legible. [[link:/tools/2215|Chemical X]] and [[link:/tools/2233|GenClass]] catch the damage before it ships. And [[link:/tools/2230|barn]] and [[link:/tools/2218|CodeConnect]] assume the honest case: you will be away from the desk when something needs a decision.

The common thread is that none of them pretend the agent is autonomous. They all keep a human in a position to intervene quickly, which is a more useful design goal than autonomy and much easier to ship.
tldr: Running agents is easy; supervising them is not. This group covers fleet observability, session naming, phone approvals, structural linting, in-browser bug detection and crash analysis, from Flightdeck and Evlat to Chemical X and ForensicDbg.
